The following paragraphs explain how. 

The government doesn't just 'have' whatever money it wants. If it did, the out-of-control inflation we have seen in some third world countries would happen here and we would become as destitute as they are.

Instead, the government takes in money in taxes, fees, fines, gifts, and tariff. It also takes in a relatively small amount of money from the sale of electricity from hydroelectric dams it has built.

So there is some money to work with. It can also borrow money, which it pays back with interest. That is how we accumulate national debt.

This is how the government gets the money that it spends on the military, government property, government employees, national parks, benefits (such as social security, SNAP, WIC), et cetera.

The Congress allots in a budget how much of the money it has will go to which programs.

This budget is developed by the members of Congress wrangling with each other. They look at whether a program is working as intended, how much it has gotten in the previous year, and other things to determine if any change needs to be made in its funding.

So, there's a process of intra-congressional negotiating to determine how much money goes where.

At the end of the process, there is a total expenditure sum. That is the amount of money the government allots out. And it allots it out for a fixed term. The government is only allowed to spend until a certain date, the end of their fiscal year. After that date, it is not allowed to spend any money, unless a new budget has already been agreed upon by congress, using the same budgetary development process.

The point is that the government AUTOMATICALLY shuts down on the 'we're out of money date' if no agreement has been reached and passed into law by that time. No party declares that they are shutting the government down. As stated above, it's automatic.

Now, if the congress is in budgetary negotiations, but hasn't reached agreement yet, it can pass what is known as a Continuing Resolution ('CR'). That's a bill allowing the government to keep spending money AT THE SAME RATE IT HAD BEEN for a fixed period of time, say, seven weeks, while they finalize budgetary details.

So, our government hit the 'drop-dead' date when we ran out of money, and it shut down. Neither party officially shut it down.

But letting matters go until the government did shut down was completely unnecessary. The House of Representatives, which is run by the Republicans at this time because they are in the majority, passed a CR with no 'riders'. That is, it didn't have any 'extra' legislation attached to it. This is commonly referred to as a 'clean' CR. Its only job was to make sure the government didn't run out of money while budget negotiations were still taking place. 

They passed this bill in late September.

These are not 'unusual'. In fact, their use is common. There were 13 of them passed without incident in the Biden administration. And there have been two passed so far in the Trump administration.

This is all very ho-hum, business as usual kind of stuff.

Except this time. 

This time, instead of passing the clean CR, the Democrat Senators, with notable exceptions (Democrat Senator John Fetterman being one of them), voted against the passage of this bill.

In all fairness, voting against a CR is not unheard of. The minority party occasionally has a budgetary issue or two they feel they need to address, and this is a way of obtaining assurance from the majority party's command structure that they will negotiate on the minority party's issue/s.
